title: Shrey Parikh Wins 2026 Scripps Spelling Bee as Indian Americans Claim 30th Title in 36 Years
excerpt: The 14-year-old California eighth-grader set a new spell-off record with 32 words in 90 seconds, extending Indian American dominance at the nation's premier spelling competition.
body:
• Shrey Parikh, a 14-year-old from Rancho Cucamonga, California, won the 98th Scripps National Spelling Bee by spelling 32 words in a 90-second spell-off — a new competition record.
  • Indian Americans have now won 30 of the last 36 Scripps championships, with five of the nine 2026 finalists coming from Indian immigrant families.
  • Parikh defeated 12-year-old Ishaan Gupta in the third spell-off in Bee history, clinching the title with the word "bromocriptine."
  • He takes home $52,500 in cash, a custom trophy, and reference works from Merriam-Webster and Encyclopaedia Britannica.

Shrey Parikh, a 14-year-old eighth-grader from Rancho Cucamonga, California, won the 98th Scripps National Spelling Bee on May 28, 2026, at DAR Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C., extending a streak of Indian American dominance that has defined the competition for three decades.

Parikh clinched the title by spelling 32 words correctly in a 90-second spell-off against 12-year-old Ishaan Gupta of Jersey City, New Jersey. Gupta spelled 25 words. The winning word was "bromocriptine," a polypeptide alkaloid derived from ergot that mimics the activity of dopamine.

A Three-Year Climb to the Top

The championship capped a multi-year journey for Parikh, who first competed at the national Bee in 2022, tying for 89th place. He returned in 2024 and tied for third. In the months leading up to the 2026 Bee, he swept the South Asian Spelling Bee, the SpellPundit National Spelling Bee, and the Words of Wisdom Spelling Bee, according to NBC Dallas-Fort Worth.

Parikh, a student at Day Creek Intermediate School, is also a competitive tennis player, percussionist in his school band, chess enthusiast, and qualified for the California state Mathcounts competition in 2026.

"I've dreamed of this moment since I started spelling in the third grade. To finally hold the Scripps Cup is surreal."

— Shrey Parikh, 2026 Scripps National Spelling Bee Champion

Indian Americans Continue to Set the Standard

Thirty of the past 36 Scripps champions have been of Indian heritage, according to NBC Washington. The 2025 winner, Faizan Zaki, was the first Muslim to claim the title. Among the nine finalists this year, five came from Indian immigrant families, including Sarv Dharavane, 12, of Dunwoody, Georgia, who finished third last year and returned with even stronger preparation.

Other Indian American finalists included Kushi Gottimukkala from Raleigh, North Carolina, who advanced by correctly spelling "Chelicerata."

Why Indian American Kids Keep Winning

The Indian American community's sustained success at the Bee reflects a cultural emphasis on linguistic precision, rigorous preparation, and competitive excellence. Dedicated spelling networks — including the South Asian Spelling Bee circuit, private coaching, and community study groups — have created a pipeline that consistently produces top spellers.

Indian Americans make up roughly 1.5% of the U.S. population, yet their dominance in the Bee is unmatched. The 2026 competition drew 247 spellers from all 50 states, the District of Columbia, three U.S. territories, and five countries including Canada and the UAE.

A New Era for the Competition

The 2026 Bee marked a return to Washington, D.C., after years at a convention center in suburban Maryland. ESPN NFL analyst and Celebrity Jeopardy champion Mina Kimes joined as the new television host. Parikh's prize package includes $52,500 in cash, reference works from Encyclopaedia Britannica and Merriam-Webster, a custom trophy with commemorative medal, and $1,000 in Delta Air Lines flight credits.

Although this was the 98th Bee, Parikh is the 111th champion — the competition has ended in ties multiple times, including an eight-way tie in 2019.
